The Minima family config contains no FLL define; only the Portenta C33 has BSP_CFG_FLL_ENABLE(0). RA4M1 Table 2.22 gives fHOCO48 = 47.52–48.48 MHz at −20 to 85 °C (±1%), widening to 47.28–48.72 at −40 to −20 °C and 47.04–48.96 at 85 to 105 °C.

claims_checked.claim: Nano Every (ATmega4809): internal OSC20M with no crystal; ±1.5% at 25 °C/3 V, ±2.0% over 0–70 °C, ±4.0% over the full range; trim step 0.75%.

Using ±2% in the drift table understates the error. The conclusion that it is the worst board still holds.

The commercial ATmega328P on Arduino boards is specified at ±10% factory and ±1% user calibration; ±2% factory applies to the ATmega328PB. This does not affect the boards' main clock, which is external.
claims_checked.source: Microchip AT15007 'Differences between ATmega328/P and ATmega328PB' Table 3-2: https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-CBDC1838-0100-4F26-A45A-134958193C3B-en-US-4/GUID-06A8DD31-E1C8-4552-95B2-959A721BD03D.html; local m328p.txt is doc 7810D

claims_checked.correction: A 40 MHz crystal is mandatory for the ESP32-S3 (guideline §3.4.1). I could not read the ±10 ppm figure in the guideline text. The Nano ESP32 uses a u-blox NORA-W106 module, so the crystal and its spec are internal to the module. Either way this is a crystal (tens of ppm), not a TCXO.

The trigger signal pulse width tFSIN_High is not less than 2us'. The page also says the OV9281 mainly uses the XVS pin. A direct fetch returned 403. claims_checked.correction: The file states all of this (in German). The 50 fps lockout is the project's own measurement, not a vendor spec. Also, the firmware's default is currentFps = 60 with a 1000 µs pulse, which by MoCapSTR's own spec is above the triggered limit.

claims_checked.claim: Firmware arithmetic: micros() has a 4 µs step on 16 MHz AVR; truncation errors are +10/0/+40/+10/+40 ppm at 30/50/60/90/120 fps; Timer1 tick errors are as listed; the drift table values are correct.
claims_checked.correction: I recomputed all values: 1/16666 µs gives 60.0024 Hz (+40 ppm); 16e6/8/16667 gives −20 ppm; 761 ppm × 3600 s is 2.74 s; the 0.07 ppm regression slope figure checks out. The regression precision assumes uncorrelated timestamp noise; correlated USB/host jitter will make it worse. The re-align branch does drop a pulse and shift the phase whenever the loop falls a full interval behind.
claims_checked.source: Calculation; MoCapSTR trigger_firmware.ino lines 108–138; ArduinoCore-avr wiring.c

vHardware.overall_answer_to_does_it_matter:
Primary sources back the main conclusion. None of the boards has a TCXO. Genuine Uno R3 and Nano V3.3 boards clock the ATmega328P from a ceramic resonator: ±0.5% initial, ±0.3% over temperature, ±0.2% aging. Its error is about 100 times that of a crystal (±20–30 ppm).

**Sync between cameras: it does not matter.** Every camera takes the same physical edge, so oscillator error affects them all equally. What is left is each camera's own FSIN-to-exposure latency, which nobody has measured and which no vendor documents. Firmware jitter of a few µs to tens of µs is also negligible.

**Absolute frame rate: it matters in two cases, and both are cheap to fix.**
- **Assuming the nominal fps.** Code that computes time as frame_index / fps, containers that store the nominal fps, or pairing with devices on their own clocks will drift by about 0.3 s per minute at ±0.5%. The fix is to fit the host perf_counter timestamps and record the measured rate, or to feed the trigger edge itself into the other device.
- **Lockout margin.** At a nominal 50 Hz, a resonator running 0.5% fast gives a 19.9 ms period, which sits inside MoCapSTR's measured 18–20 ms lockout for the InnoMaker camera. That can silently halve the frame rate, so target 40–48 Hz. MoCapSTR's firmware also defaults to 60 fps, which is above that limit.

**Corrections to the reports:**
- The ATmega328P internal RC figure was taken from the automotive datasheet. The commercial part is ±10% factory, not ±2%.
- The Nano Every's ±2% (0–70 °C) row applies only at 1.8–3.6 V. At the board's 5 V supply the guaranteed bound is ±4%, which makes it even worse than reported.
- The −761 ppm measurement came from a Pro Mini, not a verified CSTCE part. The temperatures in that article are uncalibrated internal-sensor readings (±10 °C).
- The Uno R4's ±1% HOCO is confirmed.

**FSIN voltage:**
- InnoMaker: an optocoupler input rated 3.3–5 V with an on-board 200 Ω resistor, about 19 mA at 5 V. It is 5 V-safe, but more than two cameras on one ATmega pin exceeds the 40 mA absolute maximum, so it needs a buffer.
- Arducam MIPI OV9281: 1.8 V is confirmed.
- Arducam UVC boards: the voltage is unconfirmed, so level-shift as a precaution.

A crystal or TCXO is not needed. Fix the firmware's pulse dropping and phase jumps (the re-align branch), add a pulse counter, and measure the real rate on the host.

claims_checked.claim: Genuine Uno R3 and Nano V3.3 clock the ATmega328P from a CSTCE16M0V53-R0 ceramic resonator. They have no TCXO, and the Uno's 16U2 crystal does not clock the 328P.
claims_checked.correction: I checked this in the extracted NanoV3.3.sch, which has Y1 deviceset="0011_CSTCE16M0V53-R0", and NanoV3.3.brd, which uses package="RESONATOR". The Uno text also lists the CSTCE part. I did not re-check the Murata ±0.5% / ±0.3% / ±0.2% figures against the PDF, but they match the commonly cited datasheet values.

claims_checked.claim: Joris van Rijn's data: resonator at -761 ppm with -139 Hz/°C (8.7 ppm/°C) and 43.9 Hz rms (2.7 ppm); crystal at +105 ppm with 0.06 ppm/°C and 0.04 ppm rms. Both boards were at 65-110 °C.
claims_checked.correction: The arithmetic is correct: 139/16e6 = 8.69 ppm/°C, 43.9/16e6 = 2.74 ppm, 0.97/16e6 = 0.06 ppm/°C. I could not check the source figures or the '65-110 °C board temperature' detail without web access. Each result is one board, so treat it as an example and not a distribution.

claims_checked.claim: Integer truncation of 1000000UL/fps gives +10 ppm at 30 fps, 0 at 50, +40 at 60, +10 at 90 and +40 at 120, with drift of 36 or 144 ms per hour.
claims_checked.correction: The arithmetic is right. 16666 vs 16666.67 is 0.667/16666 = 40 ppm, which is 144 ms/h = 8.6 frames at 60 fps. 33333.33 gives 10 ppm (36 ms/h). 11111.1 gives 10 ppm. 8333.33 gives 40 ppm (17.3 frames/h at 120). micros() is exactly 64 CPU cycles per 4 µs tick, and previousMicros += interval preserves the mean, so the error is exact relative to F_CPU. In practice it does not matter. At up to ±5000 ppm the resonator error is 125 times larger. Any host-measured rate absorbs the truncation error and the oscillator error together. Rates above 50 fps are also irrelevant, because the OV9281 bridge rejects every 2nd or 3rd pulse above 50 Hz (CAMERA_SPECS.md).
claims_checked.source: Re-derived; trigger_firmware.ino lines 61, 112-115; CAMERA_SPECS.md trigger table

claims_checked.claim: 'MoCapSTR hardware-trigger mode is limited to 50 fps, and that case is exact.'
claims_checked.correction: 20000 µs is exact only in MCU clock ticks. With a ±0.5% resonator the real rate is anywhere from 49.75 to 50.25 Hz, which is a period of 19.90 to 20.10 ms. That matters for the specific reason the report missed (see the lockout claim below). The documented camera lockout is 'about 18-20 ms', so 50 Hz already sits at the hardware ceiling with an unmeasured margin.
claims_checked.source: CAMERA_SPECS.md and README.md: 18-20 ms lockout, 60 Hz gives 30 FPS

claims_checked.claim: Bottom line: 'The firmware adds more timing error than the crystal-vs-resonator choice.'
claims_checked.correction: For rate error, the firmware's 0-40 ppm is about 100 times smaller than the resonator's up to 5000 ppm spec (761 ppm measured). For edge jitter, the firmware's roughly 10-20 µs is larger than the oscillator's phase noise (about 2.7e-6 × 20 ms, or 50 ns per period). But edge jitter of that size is practically irrelevant (see the jitter claim below). The sentence compares two different quantities. Read as rate error, which is the error users care about, it is backwards.
claims_checked.source: Re-derived from the report's own numbers

claims_checked.claim: Sync between cameras: oscillator error does not matter because the edge is common-mode.
claims_checked.correction: This is true as long as every camera accepts every pulse. The report missed the one way the Arduino's clock can break inter-camera sync. The InnoMaker bridge ignores any pulse that arrives within its own roughly 18-20 ms lockout, and that lockout is timed by each camera's own clock. If the trigger period gets close to the lockout, cameras can reject different pulses, and frame indices then desync between cameras. Two things shorten the period: a resonator running +0.5% fast (about 100 µs shorter), and a single late edge followed by an on-schedule edge (a one-off short interval of up to about 100 µs, see the firmware claim below). Whether this happens depends on the real lockout margin at 50 Hz, which nobody has measured. A fixed 'exact' 50.000 Hz has the same exposure to it.
claims_checked.source: CAMERA_SPECS.md lines on 50 FPS hardware limit; trigger_firmware.ino lines 112-122

claims_checked.claim: At ±0.5%, 50 fps drifts 1 frame every 4 s. Full drift table, e.g. -761 ppm gives 46 ms/min, 2.7 s/h and 26 s per frame. 2 ppm TCXO gives 7.2 ms/h.
claims_checked.correction: Every row re-derives correctly: 0.005×60 = 0.3 s = 15 frames; 761e-6×3600 = 2.74 s = 137 frames; 0.02/761e-6 = 26.3 s; 105e-6×3600 = 0.378 s = 18.9 frames; 0.02/105e-6 = 190 s. Keep in mind that ±0.5% is the worst-case spec and typical parts are better. The drift is only from nominal and has no effect on inter-camera alignment.

claims_checked.claim: micros() has 4 µs resolution, edges wobble about ±4 µs, it wraps at 71.6 min, and the unsigned subtraction handles the wrap.
claims_checked.correction: (m<<8)+t times 64/16 gives 4 µs. 2^32 µs = 4294.97 s = 71.58 min. currentMicros - previousMicros is unsigned, so it is wrap-safe. The quantization is one-sided per edge (0 to +4 µs late), so periods wobble by ±4 µs.

claims_checked.claim: The loop pass (digitalRead, millis, stringComplete, micros, serialEventRun) adds about 10-20 µs, for 4-20 µs total edge jitter.
claims_checked.correction: The range is plausible, but one detail is wrong. millis() is called only when the button state changes (line 41), so it is not in the normal pass. A normal pass is digitalRead(4) (about 3 µs), two flag checks, micros() (about 3.5 µs) and serialEventRun/Serial.available (about 1-2 µs), so roughly 8-12 µs. Edge lateness is then about 0 to 12 µs from sampling, plus 0-4 µs from quantization, plus about 5-6 µs when the Timer0 overflow ISR (every 1.024 ms) collides. That gives roughly 15-20 µs peak-to-peak, which still needs a logic analyzer to confirm. The report also does not name the UART RX/TX ISRs (a few µs per byte), which fire every second because of the host's PING.

claims_checked.claim: digitalWrite takes about 3.4-5 µs (mostly a constant delay). The LED write adds about 4 µs to the high time.
claims_checked.correction: Pins 2 and 13 are not PWM pins on the 328P, so turnOffPWM is skipped and about 3-4 µs is right. A direct port write takes 2 cycles (125 ns). The LED write sits between the trigger going HIGH and pulseStart, so the pulse is about 1004-1012 µs. That is irrelevant.

claims_checked.claim: The <FPS:N> reply is about 62 bytes, fits the 64-byte TX buffer and does not block. If the TX buffer is full, Serial.print blocks for 86.8 µs per byte.
claims_checked.correction:
Counting the bytes: 'FPS set to: 60
' is 16, 'Interval (us): 16666
' is 22, 'Pulse width (us): 1000
' is 24, for 62 in total. The ring buffer holds 63 usable bytes, and the first byte can go straight to UDR, so it fits only when the buffer is otherwise empty. 10/115200 = 86.8 µs per byte.

claims_checked.claim: A stall longer than one interval triggers the re-align branch, which drops a pulse and permanently shifts phase.
claims_checked.correction: The mechanism is correct. With a stall of 2.3 intervals, previousMicros += I leaves the lag at 1.3 I, which is at least I, so it sets previousMicros = currentMicros. Two due edges become one, and phase shifts by 0.3 I. But at 50 fps the branch is practically unreachable from this firmware. The largest single-pass output is 62 bytes, which fits the buffer, and even worst-case blocking (about 62 × 86.8 µs = 5.4 ms) is shorter than 20 ms. The likely artifact is the one the report underplays. A command handled in the pass just before an edge makes that edge late by tens to about 100 µs (String trim, the startsWith/== cascade, println). The next edge is on schedule, so one interval is short by the same amount. That happens once per second in practice, because MoCapSTR's host sends <PING> every 1.0 s for the whole session (main.py line 347). The pulse count is preserved, but at the 50 Hz lockout ceiling a short interval is what could get a pulse rejected.

claims_checked.claim: Edge jitter of µs size is negligible: 20 µs is 0.1% of a frame, 10 µs at 5 m/s is 0.05 mm, and 20 µs at 10 m/s is 0.2 mm.
claims_checked.correction: The arithmetic is right. On top of that, the jitter is common to all cameras because they share one edge, so it causes no inter-camera skew at all. The unmeasured FSIN-to-exposure latency inside each camera's bridge firmware almost certainly dominates.

claims_checked.claim: Timer1 Fast PWM mode 15, OC1B on D10/PB2, prescaler 8: 50 fps = 40000 ticks exact, 60 = 33333 (+10 ppm), 90 = 22222 (+10), 120 = 16667 (-20), 30 needs /64 = 8333 (+40), and the slowest rate at /8 is 30.5 Hz. Edges are cycle-exact with zero ISR jitter.
claims_checked.correction: Everything re-derives correctly. 2e6/60 = 33333.3, 2e6/90 = 22222.2, 2e6/120 = 16666.7 rounds to 16667 (-20 ppm), 66666 exceeds 65535 so 30 fps needs /64 (250 kHz/30 = 8333.3, +40 ppm), and 2e6/65536 = 30.52 Hz. Note that OCR1A = ticks-1 because the period is TOP+1. OC1B = PB2 = D10, OC1A = PB1 = D9, and OCR1A is double-buffered in mode 15. Fractional-N adds a deterministic ±0.5 µs period dither. It is real but unnecessary: the precision gain (about 15 µs to 0) has no practical value. The real value of a rewrite is the pulse counter and removing the late-edge/short-interval behaviour.

claims_checked.claim: Regressing host frame timestamps on frame index gives the trigger rate to about 0.07 ppm (σ = 2 ms, N = 30000, D = 600 s). A round-trip handshake gives about 1.7 ppm.
claims_checked.correction: The formula is right: σ√12/(D√N) = 0.002 × 0.02/600 = 6.7e-8, and 1e-3/600 = 1.7 ppm. But it assumes white, independent timestamp noise and a gap-free index. USB/UVC arrival times have correlated and quantized noise (MoCapSTR requests a 120 fps UVC stream, about 8.3 ms polling) and outliers, and any dropped or duplicated frame steps the index and biases the slope. Expect a few ppm, not 0.07 ppm, unless the fit is robust and drop-aware. The result is also relative to the host QPC clock, which is itself off by ±30-50 ppm. It is still easily enough to correct a ±0.5% resonator.
claims_checked.source: Re-derived; MoCapSTR CHANGELOG 'Auto' USB polling note

claims_checked.claim: skellycam's video_recorder writes the container with the nominal framerate, while video_audio_remuxer builds VFR PTS from perf_counter_ns and places audio with a single start offset.
claims_checked.correction: video_recorder.py passes fps=self.framerate at lines 120/128. video_audio_remuxer.py converts perf_counter_ns to PTS (lines 76-84) and applies a single audio offset (lines 96-101). Raw MP4 durations will be off by the trigger clock's error, up to about 18 s per hour at the ±0.5% spec, and the remuxed output is fine.

claims_checked.claim: USB-serial latency: the FTDI latency timer defaults to 16 ms, so micros() cannot timestamp host events directly.
claims_checked.correction: 16 ms applies only to FTDI bridges (the FT232RL on a genuine Nano), and it can be set to 1 ms. The genuine Uno uses the 16U2 CDC firmware, and clones use the CH340, each with different buffering. The conclusion still holds: there is millisecond-scale non-deterministic latency, so you need min-RTT filtering or regression.

claims_checked.claim: Uno R4 runs from HOCO at ±1% and is worse than a 328P resonator board. Nano Every's internal RC is ±1.5-2% and is the worst.
claims_checked.correction: The Nano Every internal-oscillator point is credible. For the R4, the datasheet HOCO band (47.52-48.48 MHz) is ±1%, but the RA4M1 USB device needs a much tighter clock, so the core or hardware may trim HOCO in ways the report did not find. Treat the R4 as 'unknown, measure it'. This does not affect the Nano/Uno answer.
claims_checked.source: ra4m1 datasheet band; not re-checked against core startup code

vReasoning.overall_answer_to_does_it_matter:
Mostly no. There is one exception that the report missed.

**Clock accuracy.**
- Genuine Uno R3 and Nano V3 boards use a ceramic resonator: ±0.5% initial spec, −761 ppm on the one board actually measured. None of these boards has a TCXO.
- Every camera's FSIN gets the same electrical edge, so oscillator error and the firmware's roughly 15–20 µs edge jitter are common to all cameras. They add no skew between cameras.
- In motion terms the jitter is under 0.2 mm even at 10 m/s.
- The integer truncation of 1000000/fps (up to 40 ppm) is irrelevant. It is about 100 times smaller than the resonator error, and anything that measures the real rate absorbs it.
- Absolute rate error only matters when something assumes the nominal fps:
  - skellycam's `video_recorder.py` writes the nominal framerate into the raw MP4s, so durations can be off by up to about 18 s per hour.
  - Devices on their own clocks that are aligned only at the start (audio, force plates, EMG) will drift.
- The fix is to save the rate skellycam measures from its `perf_counter_ns` frame timestamps (good to a few ppm against the host clock), or to route the TTL edge into the other system. A crystal or TCXO is not needed.

**The exception the report missed: the 50 fps lockout ceiling.**
- The InnoMaker OV9281 bridge ignores any pulse within its own roughly 18–20 ms lockout, and each camera times that lockout with its own clock. 50 Hz (20 ms) is the documented maximum, so 50 fps runs with an unmeasured margin.
- A resonator running up to 0.5% fast shortens every period by up to about 100 µs.
- The firmware also makes one interval short now and then. MoCapSTR's host sends `<PING>` every second for the whole session. When that command is handled just before an edge, the edge is tens of µs late and the next interval is short by the same amount.
- If the real period gets close to a camera's lockout, cameras can reject different pulses. Their frame indices then go out of step, which is a real sync failure.
- The re-align branch the report highlights, which drops a pulse, is practically unreachable at 50 fps. The worst serial blocking is about 5 ms, well under the 20 ms interval.

**What to do in the FreeMoCap integration:**
1. Add a firmware pulse counter and compare it with the frames each camera received.
2. Don't send serial commands while the trigger is running, or generate edges with Timer1. The value of Timer1 is the short-interval fix and the counter, not the µs-level jitter.
3. Measure the 50 Hz lockout margin once with a logic analyzer, or run slightly under 50 fps (for example 48–49) for headroom.
4. Record the measured rate in the metadata, never the nominal fps.

None of this needs a better oscillator.

issues.section: 3 Firmware: pulse counter, START, STOP and BURST
issues.problem: pulse_count is incremented in the TOV1 ISR, which fires at TOP→BOTTOM, i.e. at the edge itself. Two things follow. (1) START writes TCNT1=TOP. A written TCNT1 is not guaranteed to raise TOV1 on that first wrap, so the first edge may go uncounted and the 'STOP n=' total would be off by one against the logic analyzer. (2) BURST:N and an exact STOP cannot be implemented from TOV1: once TOV1 is set the next edge is already out, or less than 1 tick (8 CPU cycles) away. Also, mcu_ticks = pulse_count × (TOP+1) + TCNT1 is wrong as soon as the rate changes mid-run.
issues.evidence: Plan §3: 'A 32-bit pulse_count is incremented in TOV1 (one per rising edge)', 'START sets TCNT1 = TOP… pulse_count = 0', 'BURST:N emits exactly N pulses', 'mcu_ticks = (uint64)pulse_count × (TOP+1) + TCNT1'.
issues.fix: Count in the TIMER1_COMPA ISR. It fires once per emitted pulse at the falling edge, unambiguously. Do BURST and STOP decisions there too: on the Nth COMPA, clear COM1A/COM1B (PORTB already low) and then stop CS1x. That leaves almost a whole period of slack before the next BOTTOM. Keep a 64-bit tick_base that the ISR advances by the period that just ended, and set mcu_ticks = tick_base + TCNT1, with the usual pending-flag check under cli(). Add a CI/HIL test: BURST:1000 must give 1000 analyzer edges and n=1000.

OCR1A and OCR1B both hold the pulse width for D9/D10, so COMPB fires at the end of the pulse (~500 µs after the edge), not at T/2. Separately, 'T/2 is while no camera is exposing' assumes exposure starts at the FSIN edge, and nobody has measured that. The 18–20 ms lockout suggests the bridge firmware may relay or delay the trigger.

NXP/TI rate HCT outputs at ±6 mA (VOH spec at 4 mA), with absolute maxima of ±35 mA per output and ±70 mA through VCC/GND. Four cameras at about 16 mA is about 64 mA, and 6–8 cameras exceeds the package limit. issues.problem: Opening the port with dtr=False does not prevent the reset on most real setups. On Linux the tty layer raises DTR/RTS inside open() before pyserial can clear it, so the board always resets. The Uno's 16U2 resets on SET_CONTROL_LINE_STATE. Several CH340 Windows driver versions toggle DTR on open. Banner-wait is also needed on the old ATmegaBOOT Nano bootloader, which waits much longer than Optiboot and treats incoming bytes as STK500. The plan's 2.5 s banner window followed by PINGs can therefore send PINGs into the bootloader.

Send PING only after the banner, or after the timeout when nothing was received (meaning no reset happened). Never assume that state survives an open: always re-send PROTO, RATE, PULSE and ARM. Document the optional hardware fix (10 µF from RESET to GND on a Nano, or cutting RESET-EN on an Uno), noting that it disables bootloader uploads until removed. Drop EEPROM <SAVE>, or at least never auto-start pulses from EEPROM on boot.

If the rate changes by 50 ppm over a 30-minute take, the phase error from a straight-line fit reaches about 45 ms × 1/6 ≈ 7.5 ms. That is more than the plan's T/4 (5.2 ms at 48 Hz) residual threshold, so validation would raise false alignment failures or assign the wrong pulse_index. The host clock also drifts.
issues.evidence: Plan §4.6: 'trigger.pulse_index: the rounded fit of the camera's timestamp to the group's line'; validation requires '|residual| < T/4'. Timing report: −139 Hz/°C, 286 ppm wander over 158 h.
issues.fix: Assign pulse indices locally. Use round(Δt/T_local) between consecutive frames, with T_local taken from a sliding-window fit (e.g. 10 s), or a piecewise or Kalman fit. Keep the global slope only as the reported mean rate. Add a synthetic test with a 50–100 ppm warm-up ramp to the rate_estimator tests.

issues.problem: With V4L2 and 1 buffer, the driver has no queued buffer from grab k until the requeue at grab k+1. If one camera's publish, record or lock-step wait exceeds T, that camera's next pulse frame is dropped by the driver, and it silently receives pulse k+2 while the others receive k+1. Lock-step gating makes this more likely, because fast cameras sit holding their buffer. DSHOW ignores BUFFERSIZE and keeps a latest-sample buffer, so a grab can return a frame that arrived up to T earlier. In both cases the grab-midpoint spread no longer bounds which pulse a camera got.
issues.evidence: create_cv2_video_capture.py:62 sets CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE=1; plan §4.4 items 5 and 6 rely on the grab-midpoint spread being less than T/2.
issues.fix: In trigger mode use 2–4 V4L2 buffers and treat every frame as meaningful: never drain to the latest. Use the driver's buffer timestamp (CAP_PROP_POS_MSEC on V4L2, which is the v4l2_buffer CLOCK_MONOTONIC stamp) as the arrival time instead of the grab midpoint. Make M0 measure slip rate under load with the LED bar before choosing between ordinal and pulse-index matching.

issues.problem: The lockout may depend on the negotiated stream frame interval, exposure and resolution, not just a fixed 18–20 ms. MoCapSTR measured it only at stream fps 120 and exposure -9. Offering uvc_stream_fps='trigger' (48 fps) could put the bridge's own frame-interval gate exactly at the trigger period, so every edge becomes marginal. The plan also never checks exposure against the period in trigger mode.
issues.evidence: Plan §4.3: 'sync.uvc_stream_fps: "auto" | "trigger" | int'; MoCapSTR CAMERA_SPECS lockout measured with USB polling Auto (=120) and exposure -9.
issues.fix: In M0, sweep the lockout against stream fps (trigger rate vs 120), exposure (-11 to -6) and resolution. Do not offer 'trigger' as the stream fps unless M0 shows it is safe. Refuse or warn when exposure + readout > 0.8·T in trigger mode.

issues.section: 4.1 Detection / reconnect by USB serial number
issues.problem: CH340 clones, the most common Nano, have no iSerial, so 'remember the port by USB serial number' and 'auto-reconnect by USB serial number' fail on exactly the boards the plan targets. Ubuntu 22.04 also ships brltty, which grabs 1a86:7523 and makes /dev/ttyUSB0 disappear, and ModemManager probes ttyACM devices (genuine Uno/16U2) with AT strings, resetting the board and corrupting the protocol.
issues.evidence: Plan §4.1: 'The last good port is remembered by USB serial number'; §4.7 'Auto-reconnect by USB serial number every 2 s'.
issues.fix: Key on serial_number when present. Otherwise fall back to VID:PID plus pyserial's `location` (USB port path), or /dev/serial/by-path on Linux. Add Linux docs and a troubleshooting check covering dialout, removing or masking brltty for CH340, and a udev rule with ENV{ID_MM_DEVICE_IGNORE}="1" for the sync box.

issues.problem: The legacy <FPS:N> reply is three lines, not two. A parser that treats 'Interval (us)' as the end of the reply leaves 'Pulse width (us): P' in the stream, which then gets matched to the next command (<PULSE>). The protocol also has no request IDs. A reply that arrives after the 500 ms timeout will be attributed to the next request in both protocols.
issues.evidence: trigger_firmware.ino:62-67 prints 'FPS set to: ', 'Interval (us): ', 'Pulse width (us): '. Plan §2 lists only 'FPS set to: N', 'Interval (us): I'.
issues.fix: Define a per-command terminal line. For legacy FPS, the terminal line is 'Pulse width (us)' or 'Error:'. On a timeout, drain the input and resync with PING/PONG before sending anything else. In protocol 2, add an optional echoed tag (<SYNC#17> → '#17 SYNC …') and put 'OK'/'ERR' on a single line per command.

issues.section: 3 Firmware: rate and pulse changes while running; prescaler changes
issues.problem: Applying an ICR1 change in TOV1 is fine for TOP. But crossing 30.5 Hz requires a prescaler change, and writing CS1x mid-run (or touching PSRSYNC, which is shared with Timer0) glitches the period and breaks micros(). OCR1x is double-buffered and updates at BOTTOM, but ICR1 written in the ISR takes effect in the current period. So one period runs with the new TOP and the old pulse width, which can violate pulse < period/2. Any change made while cameras are triggered also produces one irregular period, which is exactly the lockout hazard the plan is trying to avoid.
issues.evidence: Plan §3: 'rate changes are applied in the TOV1 ISR right after BOTTOM'; 'p = 64 covers 3.8–30.5 Hz'.
issues.fix: Allow RATE and PULSE only while stopped or armed, and refuse them in protocol 2 while running ('ERR busy'). The host changes the rate by following the disable sequence (cameras to free-run, STOP, RATE, ARM, START, re-enable). If live changes are ever needed, refuse any change that alters the prescaler, and clamp against both the old and the new period.

issues.problem: 'Forced low' outputs are underspecified. FOC1x is not available in PWM modes. When COM1x is enabled, the pin takes the OC1x internal latch, which could be high if the timer was ever stopped mid-pulse. The high time is also OCR1x+1 ticks, and OCR1x=0 still produces a one-tick spike.
issues.evidence: Plan §3: '<ARM> loads ICR1 and OCR1x with the timer stopped… and the outputs forced low'; 'OCR1x = us × 2'.
issues.fix: At ARM: set COM1x=0 and PORTB1/PORTB2=0 (pins are outputs). If the latch state is unknown, briefly use Normal mode with FOC1A/FOC1B and COM=clear to clear the OC1x latches, then select mode 14 and enable COM1x. Set OCR1x = ticks−1 and enforce 2 ≤ ticks ≤ TOP/2. The real reason for mode 14 over mode 15 is that mode 15 consumes OC1A; say so.

issues.problem: Nothing stops this firmware from being compiled for boards it cannot run on. Users will try the 'worst choice' boards (Nano Every, Uno R4) as well as common fake Nanos (LGT8F328P, ATmega168, ATmega328PB). The upload docs also need the old-bootloader FQBN. The uno and nano FQBNs produce essentially the same application image. Old ATmegaBOOT also has the watchdog reset-loop bug if the firmware ever enables the WDT.
issues.evidence: Plan §3: 'CI-built .hex from arduino-cli compile --fqbn arduino:avr:nano and arduino:avr:uno'; MoCapSTR build_firmware.py uses nano:cpu=atmega328 and its flasher tries 115200 and then 57600.
issues.fix: Add `#if !defined(__AVR_ATmega328P__) || F_CPU != 16000000L` → `#error`. Report the MCU signature and F_CPU in the VERSION/STATUS reply. Ship one .hex. Document `arduino-cli upload --fqbn arduino:avr:nano:cpu=atmega328old` (57600) and the avrdude command lines for both bootloaders, plus CH340 driver notes. Do not use the watchdog.

issues.problem: The recovery covers only cameras listed in triggered_cameras.json. Cameras left triggered by MoCapSTR, AMCap or another PC, or after a failed json write, still hit the 5×1 s read failure. On DSHOW, MoCapSTR reports the open or format negotiation itself hanging in trigger mode, so a set() between open and read() may come too late.
issues.evidence: Plan §4.3: 'if the camera being opened is listed there, call cap.set(CAP_PROP_AUTOFOCUS, 0) before the capture.read()'. MoCapSTR CHANGELOG notes open/read hangs in trigger mode.
issues.fix: Also trigger the recovery when the first read fails and the camera's name or VID:PID matches the known trigger-capable list. Add an M0 item: does the DSHOW open itself block in trigger mode, and does Windows restore the AUTOFOCUS value on replug? On Linux, follow the vendor order: set auto_exposure=1 before focus_automatic_continuous=1.

issues.section: Does clock accuracy matter / §7.3 skew expectation
issues.problem: The conclusions hold. But the 'Expected: µs-scale (optocoupler and sensor wake)' skew is unsupported. The 18–20 ms lockout suggests the USB bridge firmware handles the trigger, possibly gated to its own frame or microframe timing, which could produce per-camera skew of 100s of µs or one line time. The plan also lists Uno R4 and Nano Every as poor clock choices when in fact they cannot run the Timer1 firmware at all. And the −761 ppm row is a Pro Mini, not an Uno or Nano.
issues.evidence: Plan §7 measurement 3: 'Expected: µs-scale'; 'Does clock accuracy matter' table row 'Resonator, one unit measured at −761 ppm'.
issues.fix: Say 'unknown, possibly up to ~1 ms' and give the sweep a range of 0–25 ms in 20 µs steps around the edge. Label the −761 ppm row 'Pro Mini, one unit, warm'. Mark R4 and Every as unsupported.

issues.problem: `<RATE_MHZ:48000>` reads as 48 GHz (MHz = megahertz). Splitting the prescaler/TOP math between the C and Python mirrors also invites divergence.
issues.evidence: Plan §3: 'The host sends the rate in millihertz: <RATE_MHZ:48000>'.
issues.fix: Rename it `<RATE_MILLIHZ:48000>`. Also accept `<PERIOD:p,ticks>` computed by timer_math.py, so the firmware only validates the value and the host is the single source of truth for what gets programmed.

missing_topics: The 115200 baud rate has +2.1% UBRR error at 16 MHz (U2X). Combined with a −0.5% resonator this is still under the ~4.5% 8N1 limit, but check it on the clone set. Do not change the baud rate, since legacy compatibility depends on it.

Power and grounding: the box is powered from the host USB, so a board reset or brown-out from USB hub glitches stops the pulses. Recommend a powered hub or separate 5 V feed for buffered builds, and state that the opto isolation means FSIN− can go to Arduino GND without a ground loop.

Test protocol for each oscillator type: a logic-analyzer test of D9/D10 during USART traffic and while the Identify/SYNC commands run, confirming that hardware edges are unaffected and that only the D2 mirror and the LED bar jitter.
Defined behaviour when a second process (Arduino IDE, MoCapSTR, ModemManager) opens the port during a session: that causes a reset, the pulses stop, and the device_lost path runs.
The Identify button must refuse to run on the port that is currently connected and triggering, because opening it again resets the board.
Exposure guard in trigger mode (exposure + readout vs. period) and the exposure/lockout interaction.
The order of UVC control writes on Linux (vendor order: auto_exposure=1 first, then focus_automatic_continuous=1).
Pulse count semantics written into the protocol spec: whether the counter counts rising edges or completed pulses, and whether a value read during the active pulse includes that pulse.
